statement: The axis–angle representation parameterizes a rotation in a three-dimensional Euclidean space by an ordered pair $(\mathbf{e}, \theta)$, where $\mathbf{e} = [e_x, e_y, e_z]^\mathsf{T} \in \mathbb{R}^3$ is a unit vector ($\|\mathbf{e}\| = 1$) rooted at the origin indicating the direction of an axis of rotation, and $\theta \in \mathbb{R}$ is an angle of rotation describing the magnitude and sense of rotation about the axis according to the right-hand rule; equivalently, it is represented by a rotation vector (Euler vector) $\boldsymbol{\theta} = \theta \mathbf{e}$.

symbols.meaning: unit vector rooted at the origin indicating the direction of the rotation axis (also denoted \boldsymbol{\omega})
angle of rotation describing the magnitude and sense of rotation about the axis
rotation vector (Euler vector) codirectional with the axis whose length is \theta
three-dimensional orthogonal rotation matrix in SO(3)
skew-symmetric cross product matrix associated with unit axis \boldsymbol{\omega} such that \mathbf{K}\mathbf{v} = \boldsymbol{\omega} \times \mathbf{v}
unit quaternion (versor) representation of the rotation

properties.property: The axis–angle representation is equivalent to the rotation vector (Euler vector) $\boldsymbol{\theta} = \theta \mathbf{e}$.
properties.why: both the axis and angle are encoded by a vector codirectional with the axis whose magnitude equals the rotation angle

properties.property: The representation is non-unique: a rotation vector of length $\theta + 2\pi M$ (for any integer $M$) encodes the same rotation as $\theta$, and $(-\mathbf{e}, -\theta)$ encodes the same rotation as $(\mathbf{e}, \theta)$.
properties.why: rotations are invariant under angle shifts by multiples of $2\pi$ and simultaneous reversal of axis direction and angle sense

properties.property: A vector $\mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^3$ is rotated by angle $\theta$ about unit axis $\mathbf{e}$ via Rodrigues' rotation formula: $\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{rot}} = \mathbf{v} + (\sin \theta)(\mathbf{e} \times \mathbf{v}) + (1 - \cos \theta)(\mathbf{e} \times (\mathbf{e} \times \mathbf{v}))$.
properties.why: the formula computes the exponential map action on a 3D vector directly without evaluating a full matrix exponential

properties.property: The rotation matrix $R \in \mathrm{SO}(3)$ is given by the matrix exponential $R = \exp(\theta \mathbf{K}) = I + (\sin \theta)\mathbf{K} + (1 - \cos \theta)\mathbf{K}^2$, where $\mathbf{K}$ is the skew-symmetric cross-product matrix of $\boldsymbol{\omega}$.
properties.why: the Cayley–Hamilton identity $\mathbf{K}^3 = -\mathbf{K}$ reduces the infinite Taylor expansion of $\exp(\theta \mathbf{K})$ to the Taylor series of sine and cosine

properties.property: The rotation angle and axis can be retrieved from a rotation matrix $R$ via $\theta = \arccos((\operatorname{Tr}(R) - 1)/2)$ and $\boldsymbol{\omega} = \frac{1}{2\sin \theta} [R_{32} - R_{23}, R_{13} - R_{31}, R_{21} - R_{12}]^\mathsf{T}$, or consistently via $\theta = \operatorname{atan2}(-\operatorname{Tr}(\mathbf{K}R), \operatorname{Tr}(R) - 1)$.
properties.why: the trace determines the cosine of the angle while the antisymmetric part of $R$ isolates the rotation axis scaled by sine

properties.property: The axis–angle coordinates transform to unit quaternions (versors) via $\mathbf{q} = (\cos(\theta/2), \boldsymbol{\omega} \sin(\theta/2))$.
properties.why: versor components directly correspond to half-angle cosine for scalar and half-angle sine along the rotation axis for vector parts

properties.property: The unit vector $\mathbf{e}$ rooted at the origin requires only two independent numbers (such as elevation and azimuth) to specify its direction.
properties.why: the Euclidean norm constraint $\|\mathbf{e}\| = 1$ removes one degree of freedom from three Cartesian coordinates

assumptions.assumption: The rotation axis $\mathbf{e}$ (or $\boldsymbol{\omega}$) is a unit vector in $\mathbb{R}^3$ ($\|\mathbf{e}\| = 1$) rooted at the origin.
assumptions.breaks_when: $\mathbf{e}$ is unnormalized ($\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{0}$ or $\|\mathbf{e}\| \neq 1$), which invalidates Rodrigues' formula and the matrix exponential identities.

assumptions.assumption: The motion is a rigid-body rotation in three-dimensional Euclidean space predicated on Euler's rotation theorem.
assumptions.breaks_when: The transformation includes non-rigid motion (scaling, shear, deformation) or takes place in dimensions other than three.

failure_modes.mode: Division by zero in axis extraction from symmetric rotation matrix
failure_modes.signature: Division by zero when evaluating $\boldsymbol{\omega} = \frac{1}{2\sin \theta} [R_{32} - R_{23}, R_{13} - R_{31}, R_{21} - R_{12}]^\mathsf{T}$.
failure_modes.cause: $R$ is symmetric, which occurs when $\theta = k\pi$ for integer $k$, causing $\sin \theta = 0$ and the off-diagonal skew-symmetric terms $R - R^\mathsf{T}$ to vanish.

failure_modes.signature: Off-axis terms of $R - R^\mathsf{T}$ vanish, providing no information about the rotation axis direction.
failure_modes.cause: At $\theta = \pi$, $R = 2\boldsymbol{\omega} \otimes \boldsymbol{\omega} - I$, requiring extraction of $\boldsymbol{\omega}$ via $B = \boldsymbol{\omega} \otimes \boldsymbol{\omega} = \frac{1}{2}(R + I)$ where the axis is defined only up to sign.

failure_modes.mode: Numerical inaccuracy of angle extraction for small angles
failure_modes.signature: High sensitivity and loss of numerical precision when evaluating $\theta = \arccos((\operatorname{Tr}(R) - 1)/2)$ as $\theta \to 0$.
failure_modes.cause: The derivative of $\arccos(x)$ approaches infinity as $x \to 1$.

failure_modes.mode: Non-uniqueness and many-to-one mapping in exponential coordinates
failure_modes.signature: Infinitely many rotation vectors correspond to the same physical rotation matrix under the log map.
failure_modes.cause: The exponential map $\exp: \mathfrak{so}(3) \to \mathrm{SO}(3)$ is surjective but not injective: rotation vectors differing in length by $2\pi M$ represent the identical rotation, and all rotation vectors of length $2\pi M$ in all directions map to the identity matrix.
